result: The authors report that approximately 230 K99 awards were made annually from 2006-2022, representing up to $250 million in annual investment. From 2008-2021, an average of 234 extramural K99 awards were made per year, and from 2009-2022, an average of 198 R00 awards per year.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept these descriptive statistics about the K99/R00 program. One reviewer notes the authors 'used publicly available data...to examine some of the academic characteristics' and describes the analysis as 'reasonable.' Another reviewer states the study 'examined publicly available data on the distribution of the National Institutes of Health's K99/R00 awards' without questioning these basic program statistics.

result: The authors report that about 40% of K99 awardees were women, approximately 89% of K99 awardees went on to receive R00 awards (81.8% on a rolling basis excluding 2006-2007), and men make up 58% of both K99 and R00 awardees. The same percentages of men and women K99 awardees convert their K99 awards to R00 awards, though men have received more K99 awards than women each year since 2006.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these gender-related findings without challenge. One reviewer notes the authors 'analyze the data by gender' and describes the analysis as 'reasonable.' Another reviewer explicitly states 'the conclusions are well-supported by the data, and limitations of the data and the name-gender matching algorithm are described satisfactorily,' indicating acceptance of the gender classification methodology and findings.

result: The authors demonstrate that institutions with the most NIH funding produced and recruited the most K99/R00 awardees. K99 awards were granted to 256 institutions while R00 awardees represented 357 institutions. A small number of elite institutions (Stanford, UCSF, Massachusetts General Hospital) dominated K99 awards, with 54% of all K99 awardees at 10% of institutions. Awards were concentrated in East and West coast states, particularly California, Massachusetts, and New York.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these institutional concentration findings. One reviewer states the authors 'establish a clear overview of the institutional locations of K99 and R00 awardees' and notes 'there's a clear institutional hierarchy of hiring for K99/R00 researchers that echo previous research on the rigid faculty hiring networks.' Another reviewer describes the evidence as 'compelling evidence documenting the inequalities that shape faculty funding opportunities and career pathways.'

result: The authors report temporal trends in K99-to-R00 conversion rates and institutional mobility. Until 2015, conversion rates were similar for those staying versus moving institutions, but after 2015, the activation rate for those staying at the same institution decreased. The proportion staying at the same institution declined from ~30% in early years to ~20% from 2013 onward. Self-hiring rates vary by institution type, with 36% at private institutions with large NIH funding portfolios versus 18.5% at public institutions with smaller portfolios.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these mobility findings without challenge. One reviewer notes 'the finding that researcher mobility has the largest effect on subsequent funding success is key and novel' and states 'other data supplement this finding: for example, although the total number of R00 awards has increased, most of this increase is for awards to individuals moving to different institutions. In 2010, 60% of R00 awards were activated at different institutions compared to 80% in 2022.'

result: The authors demonstrate that time to receive a major NIH award after starting an R00 ranged from 4.6 to 7.4 years, with significantly longer times for women, those who remained at their home institution, and those at institutions outside the top 25 NIH-funded. Cox proportional hazard analysis identified staying at the same institution as the greatest disadvantage (hazard ratio 0.7095, p<0.0001), followed by R00 institution funding level and gender. Each cumulative disadvantage increased median time by ~6 months and reduced overall chance by 5-6%.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these cumulative disadvantage findings as a major contribution. One reviewer states 'Men who moved to a top-25 NIH funded institution in their postdoc-to-faculty transition experienced the shortest median time to receiving a R01 award, 4.6 years, in contrast to the median 7.4 years for women working at less well-funded schools who remained at their postdoc institutions.' Another reviewer notes 'these results empirically demonstrate that even after receiving a prestigious early career grant, researchers with less mobility belonging to disadvantaged groups at less-resourced institutions continue to experience barriers.'

result: The authors report that there has yet to be a K99 awardee at a historically Black college or university (HBCU), and only two K99 awardees activated R00 awards at HBCUs out of 2,703 total K99-to-R00 transitions. The authors also document limited R01 funding at HBCUs (8 at Morehouse, 9 at Howard, 5 at Meharry, 5 at Jackson State as of April 2023).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight these HBCU findings as critically important. One reviewer states 'The authors also highlight two incredible facts: No postdoc at a historically Black college or university (HBCU) has been awarded a K99 since the program's launch. And out of all 2,847 R00 awards given thus far, only two have been made to faculty at HBCUs. Given the track record of HBCUs for improving diversity in STEM contexts, this distribution of awards is a massive oversight that demands attention.' Another reviewer notes 'documenting the pathways of HBCU faculty is an important extension of the study.'

result: The authors demonstrate institutional hiring patterns showing that most K99 awardees attain faculty positions at private institutions (62% vs 38% public), with 45% of K99 awards going to the top 25 highest funded institutions (only 24 institutions) versus 55% to 226 lower funded institutions. For R00 awards, the distribution was more even with 32% to top 25 institutions and 68% to 327 lower funded institutions. Private institutions with high NIH funding preferentially hire from other private institutions, while public institutions with smaller portfolios have hired 74% of K99 awardees from similar institutions.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these institutional flow patterns without challenge. One reviewer notes the authors 'establish a clear overview of the institutional locations of K99 and R00 awardees and the pathways for K99-to-R00 researchers' and states 'there's a clear institutional hierarchy of hiring for K99/R00 researchers that echo previous research on the rigid faculty hiring networks across fields.' The analysis is described as providing 'compelling evidence documenting the inequalities that shape faculty funding opportunities and career pathways.'

result: Using the Wapman et al. dataset, the authors analyze faculty flows showing that 296 faculty members have doctoral degrees from HBCUs out of 65,120 total faculty flows, with 529 faculty at HBCUs. Howard University granted the most doctoral degrees (116) that led to faculty appointments, with the majority (56) working at Howard. HBCU doctoral degree holders are rare at non-HBCU institutions (not exceeding 2% except at Middle Tennessee State at 3.9%). Self-hiring is common at most institutions (10-20%), and HBCUs appear to be the only institution type that hires faculty with doctoral degrees from other HBCUs. The authors document regional and institutional prestige-based hiring patterns across all institution types.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the HBCU faculty flow analysis as an important contribution. One reviewer states 'documenting the pathways of HBCU faculty is an important extension of the study by Wapman et al. (2022), and provides a more nuanced look at the pathways of faculty beyond the oft-discussed high status institutions.' The analysis is accepted without methodological concerns, though one reviewer notes 'there is a need for more refinement in this segment of the analyses' without specifying what refinement is needed.

result: The authors conclude that K99 to R00 faculty flow generally follows similar hierarchies with some deviation for specific institutions, and that prestige hierarchies in academic biomedical science align with NIH funding portfolio size. They interpret their findings as consistent with the Matthew effect and the universal core-periphery structure of hiring described by Wapman et al.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these interpretive conclusions. One reviewer notes 'some of the observed funding and hiring traits are in line with the Matthew effect in science (Merton, 1968) and in science funding (Bol et al., 2018).' Another reviewer states the findings 'enhance previous work on the relationship between mobility and ones' access to resources, collaborators, or research objects' and that the results 'empirically demonstrate' the persistence of barriers even after receiving prestigious early career grants.

result: The authors report data from a 2018 FOIA request showing that for fiscal years 2007-2017, the successful K99 award rate for white applicants was 31.0%, compared to 26.7% for Asian applicants and 16.2% for Black applicants. R00 transition rates were also higher for white K99 applicants (77%) compared to Asian (76.1%) and Black (60.0%) awardees. The authors conclude that while improvements in equity between male and female applicants have occurred, there is still a significant racial equity gap.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge these racial disparity findings. One reviewer states 'Although data on applications versus awards for the K99/R00 mechanism are limited, there exists data for applicant race and ethnicity for the 2007-2017 period, which were made available by a Freedom of Information Act request' and notes 'These results are highly relevant given the discussion of K99 award impacts on the sociodemographic composition of U.S. biomedical faculty.' The reviewer provides the specific numbers, indicating acceptance of the findings.

result: The authors speculate about various mechanisms that might explain their findings, including reduced start-up packages for internal candidates, additional service work burdens, bias in grant review, institutional support differences, and potential benefits of mobility. They suggest that the K99 MOSAIC program and targeted funding at HBCUs may increase equity, and that systemic change through NIH policy may be more impactful than individual faculty search improvements.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these speculative interpretations and policy implications as reasonable. One reviewer notes 'The findings can provide further insights for the leadership at funding and hiring institutions and science policy makers for individual and large-scale improvements that can benefit the scientific community.' Another states 'This result has important policy implications aimed at reducing funding disparities - mainly that interventions that focus solely on early career or early stage investigator funding alone will not achieve the desired outcome of improving faculty diversity.'

result: The authors acknowledge several study limitations: focus on K99/R00 awardees only (excluding non-awardees), limitation to U.S. faculty flows, lack of demographic details in public data (self-identified gender, race, ethnicity, age, degree type), and unavailability of data on unfunded K99/R00 applications.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge and accept these limitations. One reviewer states 'At no fault of the authors, the analysis is limited to only examining K99 awardees and not those who applied but did not receive the award. This limitation is solely due to the lack of data made publicly available by the NIH.' Another notes 'the limitations of the data are described adequately' and 'limitations of the data and the name-gender matching algorithm are described satisfactorily.'
